title: Coral Reefs, Acidification and Sea-Level Rise
welcome_lead: Dive among coral and rising tides — explore how warming and acidification are changing the oceans.
meta_desc: IBDP Geography Adventure: coral reefs, ocean acidification and sea-level rise.
final_note: You have visited the threatened reefs and rising shores. Oceans regulate climate but bear its costs.

concepts.def: Loss of symbiotic zooxanthellae from coral polyps under thermal stress, leaving skeletons white.
Reduction in ocean pH (around 8.2 to 8.1 since 1750) as oceans absorb CO₂.
Increase in ocean volume as water warms, contributing about half of recent sea-level rise.
Worldwide sea-level change due to variation in water volume.
Local sea-level change due to vertical land movement.
Salt-tolerant coastal forests acting as nurseries, sediment traps and storm buffers.

walkthroughs.body_html: Coral reefs occupy less than 1% of the ocean but host roughly a quarter of marine species. Repeated bleaching events on the Great Barrier Reef (2016, 2017, 2020, 2022, 2024) have damaged thousands of square kilometres. Local stressors — pollution, overfishing, sediment — compound climate change.

Approximately a quarter of anthropogenic CO₂ has been absorbed by the oceans, lowering pH by about 0.1 units since pre-industrial times — a 30% increase in hydrogen ion concentration. This hampers calcification by corals, molluscs and some plankton, threatening food webs.

Global mean sea level has risen ~20 cm since 1880, currently rising at about 3.3-4.5 mm/yr from thermal expansion plus melt from Greenland, Antarctica and mountain glaciers. IPCC projections suggest 0.3-1.0 m rise by 2100 depending on emissions. Bangladesh, Pacific atolls and major delta cities are especially exposed.
